(A) 2 moles of cyclohexane
(B) 684 g of sucrose
(C) 90.8 L of dihydrogen at STP
is:

formulas: $\text{moles of atoms} = (\text{moles of substance}) \times (\text{atoms per formula unit})$
$n = m/M$, $n = V/22.4\ \mathrm{L}$ at STP (per mole of gas)

steps.text: Cyclohexane $\ce{C6H12}$ has 18 atoms per molecule: (A) $2 \times 18 = 36$ mol of atoms.
Sucrose $\ce{C12H22O11}$ ($M = 342$): $684/342 = 2$ mol; atoms per molecule $= 12+22+11 = 45$: (B) $2 \times 45 = 90$ mol of atoms.

pitfalls: Using 22.7 L molar volume changes the number but not the order; counting molecules instead of atoms.
solution.final_check: 90 > 36 > 8.1 confirms B > A > C.

stem: Which of the following pictorial diagram most correctly represents the $\pi^*$ ($\pi$-antibonding) molecular orbital between two atoms if the internuclear axis is taken to be in the z-direction?

options.A: Diagram with two shaded lobes above the axis and a plain region below (sigma-type sketch)
options.B: Four-lobed sketch: both lobes on the left atom shaded, both lobes on the right atom unshaded (node only between the nuclei)
options.C: Four-lobed sketch: diagonally alternating phases - top-left and bottom-right lobes shaded, top-right and bottom-left unshaded (nodal plane along the z-axis and a node between the nuclei)
options.D: Three elongated horizontal lobes with alternating shading (delta-type sketch)

formulas: $\pi^*$ is formed by out-of-phase overlap of $p_x/p_y$ orbitals: a nodal plane contains the internuclear axis and another node lies between the nuclei.

steps.text: A $\pi$ MO has a nodal plane containing the internuclear (z) axis: on each atom the lobe above the axis and the lobe below have opposite phases.
Antibonding $\pi^*$ additionally has a node between the two nuclei, so phases reverse from one atom to the other.
Combined, the four lobes alternate diagonally: top-left shaded, top-right plain, bottom-left plain, bottom-right shaded - option C.
Option B lacks the axial nodal plane; A and D are not $\pi$-type.

pitfalls: Confusing $\pi^*$ with $\sigma^*$ (node only between nuclei); forgetting the axial nodal plane of all $\pi$ orbitals.
solution.final_check: Only option C shows both required nodes (axial nodal plane + internuclear node).

options.B: Ionic solutes in aqueous solution can pass through semi-permeable membrane.
options.D: To cause the reverse flow of solvent during osmosis, external pressure (any value) should be applied to side 'x'.

formulas: $\pi = iCRT$; water flows from hypotonic (lower $\pi$) to hypertonic side; a semi-permeable membrane passes only solvent.

steps.text: Side y (lower osmotic pressure) is hypotonic relative to side x - statement C is correct.

A is wrong (solutes cannot cross, so no Prussian blue forms on both sides); B is wrong (only solvent passes); D is wrong (reverse osmosis needs pressure exceeding the osmotic-pressure difference, not any value).

pitfalls: Reversing the direction of solvent flow; thinking $\ce{Fe^3+}$/[Fe(CN)6] ions cross the membrane.
solution.final_check: With $iC$ of 0.5 vs 0.4, side y is unambiguously hypotonic.

A. It can act as a reducing agent.
B. It can act as an oxidizing agent.
C. $\ce{E^3+}$ is more stable than $\ce{E+}$.
D. The standard electrode potential value for $\ce{E^3+/E}$ is positive.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

formulas: Group 13 EN (Pauling): B 2.0, Al 1.5, Ga 1.6, In 1.7, Tl 1.8; Ge 1.8. $E^\circ(\ce{Tl^3+/Tl+}) = +1.25\ \mathrm{V}$, $E^\circ(\ce{Tl^3+/Tl}) = +0.72\ \mathrm{V}$.

steps.text: A is false: $\ce{Tl^3+}$ has no accessible higher oxidation state, so it cannot be oxidized (cannot act as a reducing agent).
B is true: $\ce{Tl^3+ + 2e- -> Tl+}$ has $E^\circ = +1.25\ \mathrm{V}$ - a strong oxidizing agent.

pitfalls: Identifying E as boron (its chemistry has no stable aqueous $\ce{E^3+}$); forgetting the inert pair effect for Tl.
solution.final_check: B and D are the true statements, matching option C.

stem: Consider the given graph showing variation of reactant concentration with time. Three different reactions were started with identical initial concentration of reactants. [R] vs t: curve 1 is a straight line, curves 2 and 3 are curved decays with 3 falling faster than 2. Which of the following statement is correct?

options.A: The order of all the three reactions is same.
options.B: The rate constant of reaction 3 is larger than the rate constant of reaction 2 if the order of reaction is same for both.
options.C: The SI unit of rate constant of reaction 1 is $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
options.D: Thermal decomposition of HI on gold surface is an example of reaction 2.

formulas: Zero order: $[R] = [R]_0 - kt$ (straight line), $k$ in $\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$; for the same order, a faster fall means larger $k$.

steps.text: Curve 1 is linear, so reaction 1 is zero order - A is false, and its $k$ has units $\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$, so C is false.
Curve 3 decays faster than curve 2; if both have the same order, $k_3 > k_2$ - B is true.
HI decomposition on gold is zero order (surface reaction), i.e. reaction-1 type, so D is false.

pitfalls: Assigning $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ to a zero-order rate constant; treating HI/Au (a classic zero-order example) as curved-decay type.
solution.final_check: Only statement B survives: faster decay at the same order implies a larger rate constant.

options.A: C2: OH left, C3: OH left
options.B: C2: OH right, C3: OH left
options.C: C2: OH right, C3: OH right
options.D: C2: OH left, C3: OH right

solution.final_check: Only D-threose (option D) yields the meso (inactive) dicarboxylic acid.

stem: For the function $f:[1,\infty)\to[1,\infty)$ defined by $f(x)=(x-1)^4+1$, among the two statements:\n(I) The set $S=\{x\in[1,\infty):f(x)=f^{-1}(x)\}$ contains exactly two elements, and\n(II) The set $S=\{x\in[1,\infty):f(x)=f^{-1}(x+1)\}$ is an empty set.

steps.text: $f'(x)=4(x-1)^3\ge 0$ on $[1,\infty)$, and $f$ is strictly increasing there, mapping $[1,\infty)$ onto $[1,\infty)$; hence $f$ is bijective with $f^{-1}(x)=1+(x-1)^{1/4}$.

For (I): since $f$ is bijective, $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)\iff f(f(x))=x$. If $f(x)>x$, applying the increasing $f$ gives $f(f(x))>f(x)>x$; if $f(x)<x$, then $f(f(x))<f(x)<x$. Hence $f(f(x))=x$ forces $f(x)=x$.
Fixed points: $(x-1)^4+1=x\iff (x-1)^4=(x-1)$. With $t=x-1\ge 0$: $t^4=t\iff t(t^3-1)=0\iff t=0,1$, i.e. $x=1,2$. So $S=\{1,2\}$ has exactly two elements: (I) is TRUE.

For (II): $f(x)=f^{-1}(x+1)$ becomes $(x-1)^4+1=1+x^{1/4}$, i.e. $(x-1)^4=x^{1/4}$. At $x=2$: $1<2^{1/4}\approx1.19$; at $x=3$: $16>3^{1/4}\approx1.32$. By continuity there is a root in $(2,3)$, so $S$ is non-empty: (II) is FALSE.

pitfalls: Assuming $f(x)=f^{-1}(x)$ means the graphs meet the line $y=x$ twice without the monotonicity argument; missing the root of (II) by not testing values.
solution.final_check: Fixed points $x=1,2$ confirm (I); the sign change of $(x-1)^4-x^{1/4}$ on $[2,3]$ refutes (II), so only (I) is TRUE.

stem: If $\alpha=1$ and $\beta=1+i\sqrt{2}$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$, are two roots of the equation $x^3+ax^2+bx+c=0$, $a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}$, then $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}(x^3+ax^2+bx+c)\,dx$ is equal to:

stem: If the quadratic equation $(\lambda+2)x^2-3\lambda x+4\lambda=0$, $\lambda\ne-2$, has two positive roots, then the number of possible integral values of $\lambda$ is:

formulas: $D\ge 0$, sum of roots $>0$, product of roots $>0$

steps.text: Sum of roots $=\frac{3\lambda}{\lambda+2}>0$ and product $=\frac{4\lambda}{\lambda+2}>0$ both require $\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+2}>0$, i.e. $\lambda>0$ or $\lambda<-2$.
Intersecting with $[-32/7,0]$: $\lambda\in[-32/7,-2)$ (note $\lambda=-2$ is excluded as the equation becomes linear).

pitfalls: Including $\lambda=-2$ (the equation is then linear) or $\lambda=0$ (a zero root, not positive).

stem: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&7\\4&-2&8\\3&8&-7\end{bmatrix}$ and $\det(A-\alpha I)=0$, where $\alpha$ is a real number. If the largest possible value of $\alpha$ is $p$, then the circle $(x-p)^2+(y-2p)^2=320$ intersects the co-ordinate axes at

steps.text: Factoring: $(\alpha-8)(\alpha^2+16\alpha+40)=0$, so $\alpha=8$ or $\alpha=-8\pm 2\sqrt{6}$. The largest is $p=8$.
Circle: centre $(8,16)$, radius $\sqrt{320}\approx 17.9>16>8$, so it cuts both axes twice in principle.
On the $x$-axis: $(x-8)^2=64\Rightarrow x=0,16$; on the $y$-axis: $(y-16)^2=256\Rightarrow y=0,32$. The point $(0,0)$ is common, so there are $3$ distinct intersection points.

pitfalls: Counting the origin twice and answering 4 points.
solution.final_check: Centre $(8,16)$ with radius $\sqrt{320}$ meets the axes at $(0,0),(16,0),(0,32)$: $3$ points.

stem: For $10$ observations $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_{10}$, if $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{10}(x_i+2)^2=180$ and $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{10}(x_i-1)^2=90$, then their standard deviation is:

Subtracting: $6\sum x_i=60$, so $\sum x_i=10$ and $\bar x=1$.

pitfalls: Taking the square root of the mean of squared deviations incorrectly, or confusing $\sum(x_i+2)^2$ with a shifted variance directly.
solution.final_check: Mean $1$ and $\sum x_i^2=100$ give variance $9$, i.e. SD $3$.

stem: The shortest distance between the lines\n$\vec r=\left(\frac13\hat i+2\hat j+\frac83\hat k\right)+\lambda(2\hat i-5\hat j+6\hat k)$\nand $\vec r=\left(-\frac23\hat i-\frac13\hat k\right)+\mu(\hat j-\hat k)$, $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb{R}$, is:

formulas: $d=\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}$

steps.text: $\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\2&-5&6\\0&1&-1\end{vmatrix}=(-1,2,2)$, with $|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|=3$.

pitfalls: Sign/arithmetic errors in the cross product components.
solution.final_check: Numerator $9$ over $3$ gives distance $3$.

stem: If $\left(2\alpha+1,\,\alpha^2-3\alpha,\,\frac{\alpha-1}{2}\right)$ is the image of $(\alpha,2\alpha,1)$ in the line $\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z}{1}$, then the possible value(s) of $\alpha$ is (are)

concepts: Image of a point in a line

steps.text: Comparing with the given point: $\alpha^2-3\alpha=0$ gives $\alpha=0$ or $3$; $\frac{\alpha-1}{2}=\alpha-2$ gives $\alpha=3$. Only $\alpha=3$ satisfies both.

pitfalls: Using only one coordinate comparison and keeping the extraneous $\alpha=0$.
solution.final_check: $\alpha=3$ makes the computed image $(7,0,1)$, matching all three coordinates.

subject: mathematics
stem: Let $\hat u$ and $\hat v$ be unit vectors inclined at an acute angle such that $|\hat u\times\hat v|=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. If $\vec A=\lambda\hat u+\hat v+(\hat u\times\hat v)$, then $\lambda$ is equal to:

formulas: $|\hat u\times\hat v|=\sin\theta$; $(\hat u\times\hat v)\cdot\hat u=(\hat u\times\hat v)\cdot\hat v=0$

steps.text: $|\hat u\times\hat v|=\sin\theta=\sqrt3/2$ with $\theta$ acute gives $\theta=60^\circ$, so $\hat u\cdot\hat v=1/2$.
Dotting $\vec A$ with $\hat u$: $\vec A\cdot\hat u=\lambda+\hat u\cdot\hat v=\lambda+\frac12$.
Dotting $\vec A$ with $\hat v$: $\vec A\cdot\hat v=\lambda(\hat u\cdot\hat v)+1=\frac{\lambda}{2}+1$.

Check option A: $\frac43\left(\lambda+\frac12\right)-\frac23\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}+1\right)=\frac{4\lambda}{3}+\frac23-\frac{\lambda}{3}-\frac23=\lambda$. Hence $\lambda=\frac43(\vec A\cdot\hat u)-\frac23(\vec A\cdot\hat v)$.

pitfalls: Assuming $\vec A$ is a unit vector (the hat is only part of its name here); misreading the angle from $|\hat u\times\hat v|$.
solution.final_check: Substituting $\lambda$ back into the right side reproduces $\lambda$ exactly.

subject: mathematics
stem: Let for some $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$, $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function satisfying $f(x+y)=f(x)+2y^2+y+\alpha xy$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$. If $f(0)=-1$ and $f(1)=2$, then the value of $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{5}(\alpha+f(n))$ is:

formulas: Put $x=0$ to find the form of $f$; compare $xy$ coefficients for $\alpha$

steps.text: Now $f(x+y)=2(x+y)^2+(x+y)-1=2x^2+4xy+2y^2+x+y-1$, while $f(x)+2y^2+y+\alpha xy=2x^2+x-1+2y^2+y+\alpha xy$. Comparing the $xy$ terms: $4=\alpha$.

pitfalls: Using $f(1)=2$ to solve for $\alpha$ directly (it gives no information about $\alpha$); forgetting the $5\alpha$ term in the sum.
solution.final_check: $\alpha=4$ and $f(n)=2n^2+n-1$ give the sum $140$.

subject: mathematics
stem: Let\n$A=\{(a,b,c):a,b,c$ are non-negative integers and $a+b+2c=22\}$.\nThen $n(A)$ is equal to:

steps.text: $c$ can range from $0$ to $11$. For a fixed $c$, $a+b=22-2c$ has $(22-2c)+1=23-2c$ solutions in non-negative integers.

pitfalls: Writing the count as $23-2c$ but summing only to $c=10$, or using $22-2c$ solutions per $c$.
solution.final_check: $\sum_{c=0}^{11}(23-2c)=144$ counts each triple once.

stem: The area of the region bounded by the curves $x+3y^2=0$ and $x+4y^2=1$ is equal to:

formulas: Integrate (right curve $-$ left curve) $dy$ between intersection ordinates

steps.text: The curves are $x=-3y^2$ and $x=1-4y^2$. They meet where $-3y^2=1-4y^2$, i.e. $y^2=1$, at $(-3,\pm 1)$.

pitfalls: Integrating with respect to $x$ without splitting at the vertex, or taking the wrong curve on the right.
solution.final_check: Width $1-y^2\ge 0$ on $[-1,1]$ integrates to $4/3$.

stem: From a month of $31$ days, $3$ different dates are selected at random. If the probability that these dates are in an increasing A.P. is equal to $\frac{a}{b}$, where $a,b\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\gcd(a,b)=1$, then $a+b$ is equal to ______

steps.text: Favourable: for common difference $d$, the first term can be $1,\ldots,31-2d$; $d\le 15$. Count $=\sum_{d=1}^{15}(31-2d)=15\cdot 31-2\cdot 120=465-240=225$.

pitfalls: Counting ordered triples instead of subsets (the selected dates form a set).

subject: mathematics
stem: Let $f(x)=\begin{cases}e^{x-1},&x<0\\x^2-5x+6,&x\ge 0\end{cases}$ and $g(x)=f(|x|)+|f(x)|$. If the number of points where $g$ is not continuous and is not differentiable are $\alpha$ and $\beta$ respectively, then $\alpha+\beta$ is equal to ______

formulas: $|f|$ has a cusp where $f$ crosses zero with $f'\ne 0$; a discontinuity is automatically a non-differentiable point

steps.text: $f$ jumps at $x=0$ ($e^{-1}$ vs $6$) and is continuous elsewhere; its zeros are at $x=2,3$ with $f'(2)=-1$, $f'(3)=1$.
$f(|x|)=x^2-5|x|+6$ is continuous everywhere (kink only at $0$). $|f(x)|$ is continuous exactly on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$.
Non-differentiable points: $x=0$ (discontinuity), $x=2$ and $x=3$ (cusps of $|f|$, since $f(|x|)$ is smooth there). At $x=\pm$ other points, e.g. $x=-2$, both terms are smooth. So $\beta=3$.

pitfalls: Missing the cusp points $x=2,3$ of $|f(x)|$, or counting $x=-2,-3$ where $f$ is smooth and nonzero.
solution.final_check: $g$ fails continuity only at $0$ and differentiability at $0,2,3$: $1+3=4$.

subject: mathematics
stem: Let $A,B$ be points on the two half-lines $x-\sqrt{3}|y|=\alpha$, $\alpha>0$, at a distance of $\alpha$ from their point of intersection $P$. The line segment $AB$ meets the angle bisector of the given half-lines at the point $Q$. If $PQ=\frac92$ and $R$ is the radius of the circumcircle of $\triangle PAB$, then $\frac{\alpha^2}{R}$ is equal to ______

formulas: Angle between the rays $=60^\circ$; $\triangle PAB$ is equilateral; $R_{\text{equilateral}}=\frac{\text{side}}{\sqrt3}$

steps.text: The half-lines meet at $P=(\alpha,0)$ with directions $(\sqrt3,1)$ and $(\sqrt3,-1)$, making angles $\pm 30^\circ$ with the $x$-axis; the angle between them is $60^\circ$.
Since $PA=PB=\alpha$ and $\angle APB=60^\circ$, $\triangle PAB$ is equilateral, so $Q$ (on the bisector $x$-axis) is the midpoint of $AB$ and $PQ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\alpha$.
Circumradius of the equilateral triangle: $R=\alpha/\sqrt3=3$. Hence $\alpha^2/R=27/3=9$.

pitfalls: Using the full angle instead of half when computing $PQ$; confusing inradius with circumradius.
solution.final_check: $\alpha=3\sqrt3$, $R=3$ give $\alpha^2/R=9$.

stem: Let $A,B,C$ be the vertices of a variable right angled triangle inscribed in the parabola $y^2=16x$. Let the vertex $B$ containing the right angle be $(4,8)$ and the locus of the centroid of $\triangle ABC$ be a conic $C_0$. Then three times the length of the latus rectum of $C_0$ is ______

stem: Let $f$ be a twice differentiable function such that\n$f(x)=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{x}\tan(t-x)\,dt-\int_{0}^{x}f(t)\tan t\,dt$, $x\in\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$.\nThen $f''\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+12f'\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+f\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$ is equal to ______

steps.text: So $f(x)=\ln(\cos x)-\int_0^x f(t)\tan t\,dt$. Differentiating: $f'(x)=-\tan x-f(x)\tan x=-\tan x\,(1+f(x))$.
Solving $f'=-\tan x\,(1+f)$ with $f(0)=0$ gives $1+f(x)=\cos x$, i.e. $f(x)=\cos x-1$ (which satisfies the original equation).

pitfalls: Differentiating the first integral without the substitution, producing a wrong derivative; sign errors in $f''$.
solution.final_check: The $±\sqrt3/2$ terms cancel, leaving $6-1=5$.

stem: Two cars $A$ and $B$ are moving in the same direction along a straight line with speeds $100$ km/h and $80$ km/h, respectively, such that car $A$ is moving ahead of car $B$. A person in car $B$ throws a stone with a speed $v$ so that it (moving) hits the car $A$ with a speed of $5$ m/s. The value of $v$ is ______ km/h.

steps.text: The stone is thrown forward from car $B$, so its ground speed is $v_{stone}=80+v$ km/h.
It strikes car $A$ with relative speed $v_{stone}-100=5$ m/s $=18$ km/h.

stem: At $t=0$, a body of mass $100$ g starts moving under the influence of a force $(5\hat{i}+10\hat{j})$ N. After $2$ s its position is $(2x\hat{i}+5y\hat{j})$ m. The ratio $x:y$ is ______.

steps.text: Starting from rest, $\vec{r}=\frac{1}{2}\vec{a}t^2$; at $t=2$ s, $\vec{r}=\frac{1}{2}(50\hat{i}+100\hat{j})(4)=(100\hat{i}+200\hat{j})$ m.

stem: If $x$ and $y$ coordinates of a projectile as a function of time $(t)$ are given as $24t$ and $43.6t-4.9t^2$, respectively, then the angle (in degrees) made by the projectile with horizontal when $t=2$ s is ______.

stem: The height in terms of radius of the earth $(R)$, at which the acceleration due to gravity becomes $\frac{g}{9}$, where $g$ is acceleration due to gravity on earth's surface, is ______.

steps.text: Acceleration due to gravity at height $h$: $g(h)=g\frac{R^2}{(R+h)^2}$.

solution.final_check: Inverse-square fall to one-ninth needs three times the centre distance, so h = 2R, option C.

subject: physics
stem: A metal string $A$ is suspended from a rigid support and its free end is attached to a block of mass $M$. Second block having mass $2M$ is suspended at the bottom of the first block using a string $B$. The area of cross sections of strings $A$ and $B$ are same. The ratio of lengths of strings of $A$ to $B$ is $2$ and the ratio of their Young's moduli $(Y_A/Y_B)$ is $0.5$. The ratio of elongations in $A$ to $B$ is ______.

steps.text: Tension in $A$ carries both blocks: $T_A=3Mg$; in $B$: $T_B=2Mg$.

stem: A water spray gun is attached to a hose of cross sectional area $30$ cm$^2$. The gun comprises of $10$ perforations each of cross sectional area of $15$ mm$^2$. If the water flows in the hose with the speed of $50$ cm/s, calculate the speed at which the water flows out from each perforation. (Neglect any edge effects)

steps.text: Total volume flow in hose: $A_hv_h=30\times 50=1500$ cm$^3$/s.
Per perforation: $1500/10=150$ cm$^3$/s through $a=15$ mm$^2=0.15$ cm$^2$.

pitfalls: Divide the flow among all 10 perforations and convert mm^2 to cm^2 consistently.
solution.final_check: Area ratio gives a 100x speed-up of 50 cm/s to 10 m/s, option B.

subject: physics
stem:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as **Assertion A** and the other is labelled as **Reason R**
**Assertion A:** If the average kinetic energy of $H_2$ and $O_2$ molecules, kept in two different sized containers are same, then their temperatures will be same.
**Reason R:** The r.m.s. speed of $H_2$ and $O_2$ molecules are same at same temperature.
Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

steps.text: Average translational KE per molecule is $\frac{3}{2}kT$; equal KE implies equal $T$ regardless of container size, so A is true.
But $v_{rms}=\sqrt{3kT/m}$ depends on molecular mass, so $H_2$ and $O_2$ have different r.m.s. speeds at the same $T$; R is false.

pitfalls: Do not confuse average kinetic energy (mass-independent) with r.m.s. speed (mass-dependent).
solution.final_check: A holds via (3/2)kT while R fails because v_rms depends on mass: option C.

subject: physics
stem:
The temperature of a metal strip having coefficient of linear expansion $\alpha$ is increased from $T_1$ to $T_2$ resulting in increase of its length by $\Delta L_1$. The temperature is further increased from $T_2$ to $T_3$ such that the increase in its length is $\Delta L_2$.
Given $T_3+T_1=2T_2$ and $T_2-T_1=\Delta T$, the value of $\Delta L_2$ is ______.

steps.text: $\Delta L_1=\alpha L_1\Delta T$ where $L_1$ is the length at $T_1$.
$\Delta L_2=\alpha L_2\Delta T=\alpha L_1(1+\alpha\Delta T)\Delta T=\Delta L_1(1+\alpha\Delta T)$. Hence option D.

pitfalls: The second expansion uses the already-expanded length $L_2$, not $L_1$.
solution.final_check: L_2 = L_1(1+alpha DeltaT) multiplies the second increment, giving option D.

stem:
A uniform disc of radius $R$ and mass $M$ is free to oscillate about the axis $A$ as shown in the figure. For small oscillations the time period is ______.
($g$ is acceleration due to gravity)
[Figure: a disc hangs vertically from a horizontal axis through point $A$ at its top edge; it oscillates in its own plane about this axis.]

steps.text: Physical pendulum: $T=2\pi\sqrt{I_A/(Mgd)}$ with $d=R$ (pivot to centre of mass).

pitfalls: Use the moment of inertia about the pivot axis (perpendicular to the disc), not the in-plane diameter.
solution.final_check: I_A = 3MR^2/2 and d = R give T = 2pi sqrt(3R/2g), option C.

verification.note: First blind solve (C) incorrect; second blind solve confirms official key (A).

subject: physics
stem: A rigid dipole undergoes a simple harmonic motion about its center in the presence of an electric field $\vec{E}_1=E_0\hat{x}$. If another electric field $\vec{E}_2=2E_0(\hat{y}+\hat{z})$ is introduced to the system, what will be the percentage change in the frequency of the oscillation (approximate)?

steps.text: For small oscillations of a dipole, $f\propto\sqrt{E}$ where $E$ is the net field magnitude.

pitfalls: The dipole realigns to the new net field direction; only the field magnitude matters for frequency.
solution.final_check: Frequency scales as sqrt(3), a ~73% increase: option A.

From the circuit given below, the capacitance between terminals $A$ and $B$ shown in the circuit is ______ $\mu$F.
(take $C_1=C_2=C_3=1\ \mu$F and $C_4=2\ \mu$F.)
[Figure: $A$--$C_1$--$C_2$--$C_3$--$B$ in a row; a wire joins $A$ to the node between $C_2$ and $C_3$; $C_4$ joins the node between $C_1$ and $C_2$ to $B$.]

steps.text: The wire shorts $A$ to the $C_2$--$C_3$ node, so $C_1$ and $C_2$ are in parallel ($2\ \mu$F) between $A$ and the $C_1$--$C_2$ node.
That $2\ \mu$F is in series with $C_4=2\ \mu$F, giving $1\ \mu$F between $A$ and $B$.
This $1\ \mu$F is in parallel with $C_3=1\ \mu$F, so the total is $2\ \mu$F. Hence option A.

pitfalls: Spot the shorting wire first; it collapses two nodes and changes the topology.
solution.final_check: Topology reduces to (1+1) series 2 || 1 = 2 uF, option A.

**Reason R:** Inside the capacitor (with no dielectric medium), the free charge carriers, if placed between the plates of capacitor, experience force and drift.
Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below

options.B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

formulas: In electrostatic equilibrium $\vec{E}=0$ inside a conductor
Charges reside on the conductor surface

steps.text: In electrostatic equilibrium the field inside a conductor is zero, so all excess charge sits on its surface; A is true.
Free charges placed in the electric field between capacitor plates indeed feel a force and drift; R is true.
But R describes charge motion in a capacitor, not why a conductor holds charge only on its surface, so R does not explain A. Hence option B.

pitfalls: A true statement that is merely related to the topic is not automatically the correct explanation.
solution.final_check: Both statements are true but unrelated as explanation: option B.

subject: physics
stem:
A solenoid has a core made of material with relative permeability $400$. The magnetic field produced in the interior of solenoid is $1.0$ T. The magnetic intensity in SI units is $\alpha\times 10^5$. The value of $\alpha$ is ______.
(Free space permeability $\mu_0=4\pi\times 10^{-7}$ SI units.)

steps.text: With the core present, $B = \mu_0\mu_r H$, so $H = B/(\mu_0\mu_r)$.

pitfalls: Forgetting mu_r=400 gives 25/pi (option A), the no-core value.
solution.final_check: 1/(16pi) = 0.01989; x10^5 = 1989 A/m. Matches official key (B).

verification.note: CORRECTED 2026-10-16: independent validation against the official NTA paper showed option B is 1/(16pi) (our transcription had 10/pi) and the correct physics includes mu_r=400. Re-solved: B. Verified against official final key (B).

subject: physics
stem: A magnetic field vector in an electromagnetic wave is represented by $\vec{B}=B_0\sin\left(2\pi\nu t-\frac{2\pi x}{\lambda}\right)\hat{j}$. Its associated electric field vector is ______.

steps.text: Phase $(\omega t-kx)$ means propagation along $+\hat{x}$; $E_0=cB_0=\nu\lambda B_0$.
So $\vec{E}=-\nu\lambda B_0\sin(2\pi\nu t-2\pi x/\lambda)\hat{k}$. Hence option A.

pitfalls: Check the sign via the right-hand rule, not just the magnitude $cB_0$.
solution.final_check: E must point along -z so that E x B points along +x: option A.

A third polarizer with its transmission axis at $60^\circ$ with the horizontal axis is placed between the two existing polarizers. The ratio of the output intensities with and without the third polarizer is ______.

subject: physics
stem:
In Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment, only a few alpha particles rebound back because
A. The size of gold nucleus is very small as compared to the size of gold atom.
B. Alpha particle and gold nucleus have equal charge.
C. The impact parameter is minimum for a few alpha particles.
D. A few alpha particles have very high kinetic energy.
E. Only a few alpha particles undergo head-on collision with the nuclei.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

steps.text: B is false (alpha has $2e$, gold nucleus $79e$); D is false (all alphas have the same energy).
A is true: the tiny nucleus means most alphas pass through the empty atom.
C and E are true: only the few alphas with near-zero impact parameter (head-on) suffer ~$180^\circ$ deflection.
So A, C and E hold. Hence option D.

pitfalls: A explains why most pass through; C/E explain why the few rebound.
solution.final_check: A, C, E are true while B, D are false: option D.

stem: The de Broglie wavelength associated with an electron accelerated through a potential difference $V$ is $\lambda_e$ and the de Broglie wavelength associated with a proton accelerated through the same potential difference is $\lambda_p$. If their corresponding masses are $m_e$ and $m_p$, respectively, then the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths $\left(\frac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_p}\right)$ is ______.

pitfalls: Wavelength is inversely proportional to sqrt(mass): the lighter particle has the larger wavelength.
solution.final_check: lambda_e/lambda_p = sqrt(m_p/m_e), option A.

stem:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as **Assertion A** and the other is labelled as **Reason R**
**Assertion A:** A diode under reverse-biased condition provides very small current which is nearly independent of voltage until a critical limit at which the current increases drastically.
**Reason R:** Below the critical voltage limit, only majority charge carriers flow which increases drastically above critical voltage.
choose the **correct** answer from the options given below

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

steps.text: A is true: the reverse saturation current is nearly voltage-independent until breakdown, where it rises sharply.

R is false: in reverse bias the small current is carried by minority carriers (majority carriers are blocked by the widened depletion region); the sharp rise is due to breakdown, not majority-carrier flow.

pitfalls: Majority carriers dominate forward current; reverse current is a minority-carrier phenomenon.
solution.final_check: A true, R false (minority, not majority, carriers): option C.

subject: physics
stem: A diode has Zener voltage of $10$ V and maximum power dissipation of $0.5$ W, then the minimum resistance to be used in series with this diode for safety when it is connected to a $25$ V power supply is ______ $\Omega$.

steps.text: Worst case the diode clamps at $10$ V, so the resistor drops $25-10=15$ V.

pitfalls: Size the resistor for the worst case (diode conducting, full excess voltage across R).
solution.final_check: 15 V across R at 50 mA gives 300 ohm.

A gun mounted on the ground fires bullets in all directions with same speed. The farthest distance the bullets could reach is $6.4$ m. The speed of the bullets from the gun is ______ m/s.
(take $g=10$ m/s$^2$)

steps.text: The farthest reach is the maximum range, $R_{max}=u^2/g$ (attained at $45^\circ$).

pitfalls: Maximum range occurs at 45 degrees; any other angle gives less range.

subject: physics
stem:
Two identical small bar magnets each of dipole moment $3\sqrt{5}$ J/T are placed at a center to center separation of $10$ cm, with their axes perpendicular to each other as shown in figure. The value of magnetic field at the point $P$ midway between the magnets is $\alpha\times 10^{-3}$ T. The value of $\alpha$ is ______.
($\mu_0=4\pi\times 10^{-7}$ Tm/A)
[Figure: left magnet horizontal with S on the left and N on the right; right magnet vertical with S on top and N at the bottom; $P$ is the midpoint of the $10$ cm separation.]

steps.text: Left magnet: $P$ is on its axis at $r=5$ cm; $B_1=(\mu_0/4\pi)(2m/r^3)$ along the moment (rightward).
Right magnet: $P$ is on its equatorial line at $r=5$ cm; $B_2=(\mu_0/4\pi)(m/r^3)$ opposite to its (downward) moment, i.e. upward.
The two fields are perpendicular: $|B|=(\mu_0/4\pi)(m/r^3)\sqrt{4+1}=10^{-7}\times\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{(0.05)^3}\times\sqrt{5}=12\times10^{-3}$ T.

pitfalls: Axial field is twice the equatorial field at the same distance; get the directions right.
solution.final_check: Perpendicular 2:1 fields combine as sqrt(5), giving exactly 12 x 10^-3 T.

stem:
A circular coil of radius $2$ cm and $125$ turns carries a current of $1$ A. The coil is placed in a uniform magnetic field of magnitude $0.4$ T. The axis of the coil makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the direction of the magnetic field. The torque acting on the coil is $\alpha\times 10^{-4}$ N.m. The value of $\alpha$ is ______.
($\pi=3.14$)

steps.text: $\theta=30^\circ$ is the angle between the normal (axis) and $\vec{B}$, so $\sin\theta=0.5$.

pitfalls: Theta is measured from the coil's axis (normal), matching the formula directly.

subject: physics
stem: In a double slit experiment, when one of the slits is covered by a transparent mica sheet of refractive index $1.56$, the central fringe shifts to the position of $7^{th}$ bright fringe, obtained with both slits uncovered. If the light source of wavelength $450$ nm, the thickness of mica sheet is $\alpha\times 10^{-9}$ m. The value of $\alpha$ is ______.

steps.text: Introducing the sheet shifts the fringe pattern by $(n-1)t/\lambda$ fringes.

pitfalls: The shift counts fringes, so equate (n-1)t to 7 full wavelengths.
solution.final_check: (n-1)t = 7 lambda gives t = 5625 nm, so alpha = 5625.
